sec.title: Background
sec.p: Mangrove ecosystems recognized for their biodiversity and ecosystem services that offer unique opportunities for sustainable livelihoods such as honey production. This study characterizes the beekeeping practices associated with mangroves in Sabancuy, Campeche, Mexico, emphasizing their ecological and economic significance.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: Through 28 semi-structured surveys, we have analyzed the socioeconomic and ecological perspectives of the local beekeepers operating in these coastal environments. The surveyed beekeepers, with an average age of 49 years and 23.6 years of experience, primarily engage in complementary honey production, leveraging both migratory and stationary apiary systems. Hive management practices include queen replacement, artificial feeding, colony division, and adherence to organic certification protocols.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: The study highlights an annual average honey production of 65.37 kg per colony, with peak yields occurring during the transition from dry to rainy seasons (May–June). Integrating floral phenology and phylogenetic frameworks the principal plant resources supporting honeybees, enhancing the sustainability of the mangrove-based beekeeping.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Apiculture not only produces economic opportunities for the local communities; but also contributes to conservation goals by fostering biodiversity and ecosystem restoration. These findings underscore the potential of mangrove beekeeping as a replicable model for sustainable development in other coastal regions worldwide with similar ecosystems. Furthermore, this research seeks to bridge critical knowledge gaps about Apis mellifera in mangrove ecosystems by addressing socio-ecological factors influencing honey production, evaluating its benefits for local communities, and exploring its role within broader conservation strategies.

sec.title: Background
sec.p: Mangrove ecosystems have tropical and subtropical distribution, these are globally recognized for their exceptional biodiversity, coastal protection, and carbon sequestration capabilities; despite these benefits, they remain among the most threatened ecosystems due to anthropogenic activities and climate change [1–3]. The socio-ecological dynamics underlying mangrove honey (MH) production remain underexplored, particularly in the context of floral resource availability, hive management, and their alignment with conservation strategies. In addition to this knowledge gap, there is an implicit heterogeneity across mangrove ecosystems throughout their natural distribution [4–7]. Therefore, to build a robust frame of reference, it would be ideal to evaluate each region for future comparative or integrative studies in Mexico and/or areas with mangrove-based beekeeping [8].

However, integrating sustainable practices, such as mangrove-based beekeeping, provides a unique opportunity to bridge ecological restoration, socioeconomic resilience, and of course, the ethnobotanical knowledge implicit in this practice. For instance, the Sundarbans region of India and Bangladesh; home to the largest mangrove forest in the world, highlights the ethnobotanical knowledge, ecological, and economic significance of MH, particularly its lucrative potential as a niche commodity [9]. Studies on the MH indicate that honey production fosters biodiversity while providing economic resilience for local communities [10–14]. Mangrove honey is also produced in Latin American countries, but its value has not been properly estimated. For example, in Cuba, around 10,212 tons of the MH was produced in 1983; but, its origin was not confirmed through pollen analysis [14, 15]. In Nicaragua, production is low, and in the Dominican Republic, hives are moved from dry forests to mangroves to take advantage of the flowering of the black mangrove Avicennia germinans (L.) L., without much discussion about other food sources [16]. The rural communities in the coastal areas with mangroves in Nicaragua have a low production of MH, between 10 and 15 kg per hive [17]. However, in the Dominican Republic, the transfer of hives from the dry forests to the areas where mangroves is protected [18] as a way to keep the hives in optimal conditions (without artificial feeding, taking advantage of the flowering of A. germinans between July and August), very little or nothing is mentioned about other floral species that could also contribute to the diet of bees before or after the flowering of A. germinans [16].

In the mountain forests of Canelones, Uruguay [19], and the coffee agroforestry systems in Veracruz, Mexico [20]; research-derived ethnobotanical information has enabled the improvement of migratory practices, such as transhumance, by aligning them with seasonal floral availability (using a floral calendar) to optimize honey production. This highlights necessity of identifying key floral resources and their seasonal availability to support sustainable beekeeping practices. Similarly, research into floral resources available to A. mellifera in mangrove habitats can inform frameworks for managing hive migrations adapted to mangrove settings, as has been reported in semi-natural agricultural systems [21].

As far as we know, there are few or almost no available phylogenetic approaches related to floral calendars. Integrating a floral calendar with a phylogenetic framework can reveal phylogenetic structures or topologies that summarize evolutionary convergences between plants and pollinators in specific areas [22]. Such approaches also help evaluate the most important lineage interactions [23] at the family, subfamily, or genus level, while laying the groundwork for macroevolutionary studies [24]; such as tracing the origin of melliferous flora in specific environments like mangroves.

From the ethnobiological knowledge in mangrove ecosystems of Campeche, Mexico, allows the development of activities such as beekeeping. While mangrove conservation provides benefits, its socioeconomic impact on honey production remains unclear. Assessing floral phenology and hive management in mangroves could address this gap. Existing research on mangrove ecosystems has predominantly focused on restoration practices [25, 26] or the ecological roles of pollinators, such as A. mellifera [27]. While these studies provide critical insights, they rarely integrate socio-ecological and phylogenetic frameworks to understand the interactions between honey production and floral phenology. This gap limits the development of sustainable practices that optimize hive management and floral resource utilization in mangrove habitats.

Others studies indicate that mangrove restoration and sustainable utilization can yield significant incomes while preserving critical ecosystem services, including biodiversity and coastal protection [25, 28]. Beyond local community benefits, mangrove beekeeping enhances global conservation efforts and promotes economic development through the production of high-value honey, renowned for its unique flavor, which is increasingly sought after in gourmet cuisine [9]. Classified as a monofloral product (when primarily derived from one type of flower or taxon), MH fetches premium prices in niche markets due to its distinct flavor profile and high antioxidant content [29, 30].

Mexico ranks fourth in the world in mangrove conservation; and, studies on honey from these ecosystems have focused on its physicochemical characteristics, botanical origin, commercial acceptance, and gastronomic uses [31–33]. An exceptional case is that of Veracruz, where community beekeeping projects in mangroves are promoted for training, awareness, and conservation purposes [34].

Ecological studies on mangroves, such as those by Celebrezze and Paton [27], Dohzono and Yokoyama [35], and Diller et al. [36], provide us with valuable insights into potential ecological trade-offs involving A. mellifera. These studies emphasize the need for context-specific management, highlighting that while A. mellifera can enhance pollination and ecosystem stability, it may also compete with native pollinators or face efficiency limitations under certain conditions. Integrating sustainable restoration practices and enhancing floral resources can mitigate these challenges and fostering coexistence. While the previous studies provide valuable insights into the role of A. mellifera in pollination and ecosystem stability, significant gaps remain regarding the socio-ecological dynamics of mangrove-based beekeeping. These include technological limitations and perceptions of insufficient floral diversity, particularly in rural areas where traditional practices dominate [37, 38]. By tailoring the results of this research to adapt to these technological and ecological constraints, it seeks to demonstrate that such limitations need not hinder the potential of mangrove beekeeping. The objective of this study has been to characterize the socioeconomic and ecological perspectives of the local honey production in the mangrove ecosystem of Sabancuy, Campeche, Mexico, as a potential economic alternative for rural-coastal communities. Furthermore, a floral calendar has been constructed for the melliferous flora of the local mangroves ecosystem to better understand the flowering patterns of the melliferous flora across the honey production cycle.

sec.title: Study area
sec.p: The Yucatán Peninsula (YP, made up of the states of Campeche, Yucatán, and Quintana Roo) is a region of great beekeeping importance, since it exports 95% of its honey production to the international market [39]. Honey is obtained mainly from the dry and humid forests of the region, using traditional techniques, family apiaries, and on a small scale; this activity represents a source of self-employment and economic income for peasant families, as well as a way to maintain their link with the countryside [40]. Around 2400 plant species have been recorded in the region [41], of which 921 have honey potential and 30 are considered of great importance for beekeeping, coming from dry and humid forests [42]. However, most studies have ignored mangrove vegetation as a provider of floral rewards (nectar and pollen) for bee feeding or honey production.

Sabancuy was selected due to its accessibility to a network of local beekeepers and its ecological significance within a Ramsar site, which offers a unique opportunity to explore the interplay between apiculture and mangrove conservation. Sabancuy (18°58′21″N, 91°10′40″W), Campeche, an area within the Isla Aguada Boca de Pargos Ramsar site, was selected as the focal point for this study (Fig. 1). This region is recognized for its extensive mangrove ecosystems and vital role in biodiversity conservation; dominated by mangrove species such as A. germinans, Conocarpus erectus L., Laguncularia racemosa (L.) C.F. Gaertn., and Rhizophora mangle L., it offers an ideal landscape to explore the integration of sustainable livelihoods with environmental conservation [43] (Figs. 2 and 3). Mexico’s commitment to mangrove preservation aligns with global initiatives such as the Ramsar Convention and the United Nations Decade of Ecosystem Restoration (2021–2030). These initiatives emphasize reversing ecosystem degradation, highlighting the potential of mangrove-based practices like honey production to bridge conservation efforts and socioeconomic resilience. Sabancuy’s approach in this research underscores its role as a model system for investigating these dual benefits and fostering sustainable conservation strategies.Fig. 1

sec.title: Survey design
sec.p: To evaluate the socio-ecological aspects of approximately 60 beekeepers (an estimate based on interviews with producers, since there is no information on the total number of beekeepers and apiaries established in the mangrove), 28 interviews were conducted with available participants, representing nearly half of the estimated population of MH producers in Sabancuy (Table S1). Lacking formal records and derived from logistical constraints associated with the availability of the beekeepers (because most of the surveyed individuals engage in additional occupations outside of beekeeping, which often require them to leave Sabancuy), the sampling approach relied on snowball sampling, which is particularly effective for accessing hard-to-reach populations [44, 45]. This method has been widely applied in socio-ecological studies to capture detailed insights into complex systems with limited formal records, as demonstrated in research involving socio-ecological systems such as the beekeeping industry, stakeholders’ perspectives on apiculture, and competition dynamics between wild and managed bees [46]. These examples underscore the utility of snowball sampling in navigating the challenges of gathering data from dispersed communities engaged in apiculture within ecological settings.

The survey period was conducted between August 2022 and August 2023, covering 1 year or a full beekeeping cycle, which allowed the data to capture critical floral phenology stages and seasonal variations in honey production. The survey included questions of the producer, age, gender, number of apiaries, number of hives, motivations for dedicating themselves to the production of MH, and flowering periods of mangrove flora (including all mangrove species reported to Yucatán Peninsula) (Table S1). These questions were designed to align with the study’s objectives of understanding the socioeconomic and ecological aspects of the MH production.

sec.title: Data analysis by beekeeper and by apiary
sec.p: For the purpose of data analysis from the surveys, two levels of aggregation were considered (beekeeper and apiary). In the first case, the total and average of the numerical variables of interest were taken into account (e.g., annual production, number of apiaries, number of colonies, etc.), together with the variation in meters between the apiaries. New categories were also created for categorical variables that presented heterogeneity within the same beekeeper (e.g., mobility of the boxes); classified into three types: (a) fixed, (b) migratory, and (c) fixed + migratory (mixed). In the second case, it was assumed that the apiaries were homogeneous with respect to their dimensions, characteristics, and management. The observations at the apiary level were used for each variable.

To explore the relationships between numerical and categorical variables, and in particular, identify those that were associated with annual honey production, various statistical analyzes were carried out with the R programming language [47]. For numerical data, a pair plot created with the GGally package [48] was used, which includes histograms, correlations, and trend lines with scatter plots. Additionally, a principal component analysis (PCA) was performed using the prcomp function in R. For categorical data, annual production was classified into four distinct levels (low, medium, high, and very high) using the cut function in R, and the data were transformed into factors with the dplyr mutate function [49]. Components explaining at least 70% of the cumulative variance were retained for further analysis. A multiple correspondence analysis (MCA) was performed with these data using the Factoextra [50] and FactoMiner [51] packages. For the MCA, variables were transformed into factors, and eta-squared (η2) values were calculated to evaluate the contribution of each variable to the main dimensions, with a significance threshold set at 0.05.

Meanwhile, qualitative data (e.g., motivations for beekeeping and perceived challenges) were analyzed to identify patterns and interrelations, visualized using chord diagrams created with the Origin Pro10.0.5.157 software [52]. This mixed-methods approach, commonly applied in socio-ecological research [53, 54], enabled the study to corroborate quantitative findings with qualitative insights, providing a holistic perspective on the factors influencing MH production.

For instance, while quantitative data highlighted variations in honey production levels, qualitative data provided contextual explanations such as the impact of floral resource availability, beekeeping practices, and external occupations of the local beekeepers. Such integration of data types is critical for addressing complex socio-ecological questions and advancing sustainable management practices within the beekeeping industry.

sec.title: Floral calendar
sec.p: We constructed a comprehensive floral calendar by filtering the dataset presented by Zúñiga-Díaz et al. [42], which encompasses melliferous flora across all ecosystems of the Yucatán Peninsula. This filtered dataset specifically focused on species occurring in mangroves helped in the assessment of their flowering patterns throughout the annual honey production and across different seasons such as: January–May (dry = prolonged dry period of reduced or zero rainfall), postharvest from June to September (rainy = high humidity with rainfall), and preharvest from October to December (northern or nortes = period of north winds, with high humidity and rain or non-humid, with low temperature) [42].

For the above, we used the approach of Jin and Qian [55] that implements the U. Phylomaker package for the R programming language, a mega phylogenetic tree of angiosperms provided by the same author (https://github.com/megatrees/), which is updated with respect to the phylogenetic positions of angiosperms, as well as their nomenclature, also, the list obtained from Zuñiga-Díaz et al. [42]; was structured in a database to be used as an output file. Following the author’s suggestions, the node type 1 and scenario 3 options were used, in order to link the listed taxa at the genus and family level based on the angiosperm mega tree. The resulting tree was fed with information on flowering such as absence (when they are not in bloom) and presence (in bloom) for each month. These annotations were incorporated into the tree using TreeViewer, a handy software for editing and visualizing phylogenetic trees [56].

sec.title: Beekeepers
sec.p:
The average age of the beekeepers surveyed was 49 years, with a range between 21 and 77 years. The average number of apiaries per beekeeper was 3, with a minimum of one and a maximum of 12 (Figs. 4 and 5). The average number of colonies per apiary was 28, with a minimum of 15 and a maximum of 50. The average honey yield per colony per year was 65 kg. Majority of the local beekeepers (78%) had some level of primary and/or secondary education. Around 15% of the beekeepers interviewed had high school and/or bachelor´s degree, and the remaining 7% had no formal education (Fig. 4). The average price of honey sold in bulk was 52 Mexican pesos per kilogram (3 USD), and the price to the final consumer was 99 Mexican pesos per kilogram (5 USD).Fig. 4

The results of the exploration of numerical data per apiary indicate the existence of statistically significant correlations between the variables “Beekeeper’s age” (BA) versus “Apiary age” (AA), “BA” versus “Apiary maintenance frequency” (AMF), “Mangrove bee boxes” (MBB) versus “Beekeeping experience” (BE), “AA” versus AMF presented significant correlations (Fig. S1). Principal component analysis (PCA) showed that PC1 and PC2 explained 65% and 23% of the variability in the data, respectively; providing a comprehensive overview of the main patterns influencing honey production (Fig. 6). The variables AP, BA, AA, and AMF had the highest values in the first component (PC1), indicating their strong contribution to patterns of honey production and beekeeping practices, both for the data per beekeeper and per apiary. This suggests that these variables play a crucial role in the overall variance captured by PC1. For the second component (PC2), the variables MBB, BE and AP presented the highest values. The results suggest that the variables AA, AMF, BA, BE, and MBB are the ones that are most closely related to the annual honey production (AP) variable.Fig. 6

Including these correlation coefficients provides a clearer understanding of the strength and significance of these relationships. With the data per beekeeper, it was found that the variables “AP” and “MBB,” and “MBB” and “BE” were significantly correlated (Fig. 6). sec.title: Categorical variables
sec.p:
The results of the multiple correspondence analysis (MCA) showed that the annual production (AP) of honey that has been classified under four distinct categories was identified as one of the most relevant variables. The AP variable had the greatest contribution to dimensions 1 and 2 that explained 14.3% and 9.8% of the total variance, respectively (Table 3). Various groupings in the variables were identified with a confidence level of 95% (Fig. S2). sec.title: Floral calendar
sec.p:
A phylogenetic hypothesis was obtained from the species identified by beekeepers as resources for bees, as well as those previously reported in the literature [58]. The resulting tree had 101 terminals, 196 nodes, of which only 17 presented continuous or almost continuous flowering (throughout the year or 11 months). On the other hand, 19 species, not counting the previous ones, had a flowering during the northern season and 11 species, not considering the previous ones, had a flowering during the rainy season (Table 3 and Fig. 7). These last two seasons or apibotanical cycles are considered critical periods for the forage resources of A. mellifera, according to the dates mentioned by beekeepers and the literature [54]. This is particularly significant as these cycles coincide with reduced floral availability in the ecosystem, potentially influencing colony strength, honey yield, and the sustainability of beekeeping practices. Also, the data indicate the independent evolution of the mangrove habit or condition, as well as the overlap between the blooms of all these entities. sec.title: Producer age
sec.p: The age of the beekeepers in this study demonstrated significant correlation with the age of the apiaries; derived from apiary inheritance and knowledge transfer at a young age. The suggested age range of the participants indicates that beekeeping practices and experiences may vary significantly; thereby, potentially influencing both traditional and modern techniques used across various age groups investigated.

The average age of the beekeepers surveyed in this study was 49 years. It not only highlights the generational diversity within the beekeeping community; but also suggests the potential differences in their access to the available resources, adaptation to innovations, and continuity of their practices. These data coincide with what was reported by other studies carried out in the YP, which indicate that the majority of beekeepers are adults over 40 years of age [56–58]. This may be because young people have less interest and/or access to the activity; or perhaps because they migrate in search of better available job opportunities [59]. The advanced age of producers can limit the adoption of technological innovations that improve yields but can also reflect the experience and accumulated knowledge about the hives management and the environment [60]. Regarding gender, it was observed that mangrove beekeeping is predominantly carried out by men (71%), while women represent 29% of the producers. This difference may be related to cultural, social, and/or economic factor(s) that condition women’s access and participation in the activity [61].

sec.title: Education level
sec.p: The educational level of the beekeepers interviewed was low since 78% only had primary or secondary education, and even 7% had no education. This result is similar to that found by other authors who have studied beekeeping in the YP, where an average of 4–5 years of schooling has been reported [56, 62]. Educational level has been shown to positively influence technology adoption and productivity in the rural sector [63]. In case of honey production in southwestern Ethiopia, there is a correlation between educational level and honey production yield; demonstrating that an increase by an in educational level (or schooling) of respondents, production or yield increased by 4 kg [64]. However, there are also other variables that intervene with the number of colonies per producer or honey production per colony per year, such as access to credit, technical assistance, social organization, floral diversity, and environmental quality [58]. Greater emphasis on training and educational initiatives tailored to local contexts could foster improved productivity and sustainability in the region.

sec.title: Number of apiaries per producer
sec.p: The average number of apiaries per producer in the town of Sabancuy was 3, with a minimum of one and a maximum of 12 apiaries. These data coincide with what is reported by other studies carried out in the YP, which indicate that the average number of apiaries per producer ranges between 2 and 3 [56, 65, 66]. These values are lower than those of other regions of the country, where beekeepers usually have more apiaries and more colonies per apiary. This is because the YP is characterized by having more extensive than intensive beekeeping, based on the use of the floral diversity of the forest and mangrove, and with less use of local inputs and available technologies [67]. Encouraging diversification and the adoption of innovative practices could allow producers to balance traditional techniques with higher yields.

sec.title: Number of colonies per apiary
sec.p: The biplots obtained (Fig. 6a and b) indicate that this is one of the variables most associated with honey production, and they coincide with what is reported in the literature. That is, the average number of colonies per apiary in mangrove vegetation of the town of Sabancuy was 28, with a minimum of 15 and a maximum of 50. These data are similar to that reported earlier by Martínez-Puc et al. [59]; who reported that on an average of 28 colonies per apiary in medium stature tropical forest in the town of Santo Domingo Kesté, Campeche. These values are higher than those of other regions of the country, where the average number of colonies per apiary is usually less than 20 [67]. This is because the YP has a greater availability of floral resources that allow maintaining a greater density of colonies per apiary, without excessive competition for food [68].

sec.title: Production yield
sec.p: The yield obtained in Sabancuy was 65.37 kg of honey per colony per year. This is, higher than the national average of 27.77 kg, calculated on the number of colonies (2,315,355) and the volume of honey production (64,320,371 kg) reported in Mexico in 2022. It should be noted that Campeche is the second honey producer nationally, after Yucatán, and that both states contribute about 35% of the national volume, concentrating between 30 and 35% of the country’s colonies [67, 69]. Honey production depends on various factors, among which precipitation and temperature stand out, which influence the nectar production of the vegetation [68]; as well as climatic, anthropogenic, and technological factors, that determine management practices and the adoption of innovations by beekeepers [70]. The strategic use of mangrove areas, which offer floral resources throughout the year, appears to be a critical factor for the observed yields. Future studies should evaluate how these resources can be leveraged sustainably without impacting biodiversity. The location of the apiaries in the mangrove area is a determining factor for the success of beekeeping since it implies the use of the floral resources available throughout the year. It is important to note that 92.8% of the beekeepers interviewed stated they had previous experience in riverside fishing; which has allowed them to acquire empirical knowledge about the ecological functioning of the mangrove. This knowledge translates into appropriate management practices, such as separating apiaries between 300 and 5000 m, to avoid competition for food between bee colonies.

The literature review plus the review of the floristic list conducted in the study area recorded 101 species of plants associated with the mangrove, of which 17 presented continuous or almost continuous flowering, 19 flowered during the northern season, and 11 during the rainy season. These species represent a source of nectar and pollen for A. mellifera in periods of resource scarcity in other surrounding forests. There are studies on the beekeeping importance of forest species in other regions [71]. However, this study includes a novel approach with the first phylogenetic representation of the honey flora of a particular area that allows the selection of species and adaptation to potential maintenance strategies for beekeepers.

This approach highlights how certain plant lineages, despite belonging to distinct families, may converge in key floral traits relevant to honey production; per se, the calendar with phylogenetic approach providing us with necessary information. It can be mentioned for example that, from the student community interested in biological careers, such as beekeeping and looking for alternatives for production, the topologies allow opportunities to address future topics as macroevolution [22, 24]; also, conservation issues are available, as phylogenetic diversity (e.g., index of Faith; [72]) to conservation are not only based on the number of taxa. It also allows us to consider the taxa that provide greatest resources and evolutionary history for the MH flora. Furthermore, these approaches should be reproduced through a forest gradient, which would allow us to understand evolutionary affinities, regarding their biogeography and/or ecophysiology. This last topic should be one of the most important points to evaluate; since some plant elements may not behave the same in the forest gradient, or have variations in floral phenology, which unfortunately could be linked to accelerated climate change [73].

sec.title: Price
sec.p: The price–cost relationship expresses the ability to generate benefits between economic units (companies) by linking market prices and the production costs of the good [74]. Therefore, the sales price and production costs determine the profitability of the concerned activity. In this sense, the honey obtained by Sabancuy producers has two marketing alternatives, to sale in bulk. One has been selling to the commission agent, where the average price was 52 Mexican pesos per kilogram (3 USD); or sold it in retail directly to the final consumer with an average price of 99 Mexican pesos per kilogram (5 USD). However, in other parts of Mexico (such as Tabasco), the price per liter of MH through direct sales averages around 130 Mexican pesos (6 USD) [75].

The price paid by the commission agent is due to the fact that the majority of the product is destined for the international market. The international price is determined by the volume of global supply and the average annual demand. The sales price is higher when honey is marketed directly to the final consumer; since the number of processes involved in marketing is reduced.

sec.title: Limitations and future research
sec.p: Beekeeping is an agricultural activity of great importance for Mexico, especially for the YP, which is the main honey producing and exporting region to the European market [66]. However, beekeepers have had to adapt to various changes that affect the management and profitability of the activity, such as the Africanization process, international honey price fluctuations, climate change, and habitat degradation and/or loss [76]. In this sense, the data explored in mangrove beekeeping showed, in a few cases, a statistically significant importance; however, in some cases, due to their nature, we consider that in the future, they should be addressed with greater sampling or geographic gradients, which would allow testing probabilistic models with the variables or conditions that statistically favor and/or harm honey production, allowing us to go beyond the descriptive statistics.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Mangrove-based beekeeping in Sabancuy positively contributes to both the environment and the local economy, standing out for its high honey yield (65.37 kg/colony/year), which surpasses the national average. This success is attributed to the strategic use of floral resources available year-round, which also promotes the conservation of ecosystem services such as coastal protection, carbon sequestration, and the maintenance of marine biodiversity.

The study underscores the importance of both migratory and non-migratory apiaries in adaptive colony management, as this activity has the potential to reduce competition for floral resources during critical periods. Moreover, statistical analyses revealed strong correlations between variables such as beekeeper age, apiary age, maintenance frequency, beekeeping experience, and honey production, indicating that long-term, experience-based knowledge and consistent apiary care are key factors influencing productivity. These findings highlight the role of intergenerational knowledge transfer and the value of accumulated experience in enhancing sustainable apiculture. The phylogenetic framework provides valuable insights for future macroevolutionary studies, such as investigating the origin of melliferous flora; thereby identifying the most significant melliferous flora utilized by A. mellifera while emphasizing the importance of preserving their evolutionary lineage.

It is essential to continue investigating geographic gradients and phenological variations, particularly in the context of climate change, to understand how these factors might impact the sustainability of mangrove-based beekeeping. Furthermore, determining which of the four mangrove species is most representative in the production of MH could involve analyzing the presence of higher pollen grain densities from a particular mangrove species in honey samples. Our study demonstrates that beekeeping in the mangroves habitat can constitute a long-term, sustainable conservation strategy for coastal ecosystems; and serve a potential source of employment for the local fishermen in the closed seasons (May–July), when their income substantially decreases.

Finally, conducting a profitability analysis is recommended to assess the economic potential of mangrove-based beekeeping in the region to link sustainable honey production with national and international markets, aligning with global conservation goals and the Sustainable Development Goals.
